# Option A: three short cards and one question

## Where This Leaves Us {.smaller}

::: {.card-row}
::: {.card .green}
<span class="card-title">Re-use is highest in HTA</span>

One recipe, many diners, many cuts. A machine-readable recipe pays back on every re-cook, and nowhere is it re-cooked more.
:::
::: {.card}
<span class="card-title">A shared standard is what makes shared tooling possible</span>

Thousands of records to navigate, trace and diff. Sponsors need that for QC, assessors to find what they asked for. Nobody builds a viewer for an in-house format.
:::
::: {.card .orange}
<span class="card-title">Nobody has asked, and every field has a cost</span>

No regulator or assessor names ARS. The metadata is paid for by a programmer on a deadline, for a reader they will never meet.
:::
:::

::: {.big-statement}
What would we want to achieve, and what would it cost to capture?
<span class="sub">Reproducibility, efficiency to reproduce, or legibility for a reviewer and for a machine: pick the goal before picking the metadata. Over to the discussion.</span>
:::

# Option B: two columns, why it pays and what it costs

## Where This Leaves Us {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .green}
<span class="card-title">Why it could pay back</span>

- The same recipe is re-cooked for more diners in HTA than anywhere else in the lifecycle
- Thousands of result records become navigable, traceable and diffable, for the sponsor's QC and the assessor's search alike
- A record a machine can cite is a record a reviewer can check
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .orange}
<span class="card-title">What it would cost</span>

- Vocabulary HTA has and ARS does not: PICO, comparator source, criteria, provenance, destination
- Every field filled by a programmer on a deadline, for a reader they will never meet
- No regulator or assessor has asked for it, so the business case is internal until that changes
:::
:::
:::

::: {.big-statement}
What would we want to achieve, and what would it cost to capture?
<span class="sub">Pick the goal before picking the metadata. Over to the discussion.</span>
:::

# Option C: one statement, three lines, spoken not read

## Where This Leaves Us

::: {.big-statement style="font-size: 2.2em; margin-top: 1.2em;"}
One recipe. Many diners. Who writes the menu?
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.35em; line-height: 1.9; margin-top: 1.2em; color: #2c3e50;"}
HTA re-cooks the recipe more than anyone, and can run none of it.<br/>
A shared recipe is what makes a shared kitchen possible.<br/>
Nobody has ordered it yet, and every line of the recipe costs someone.
:::

::: {.big-statement style="font-size: 1.3em; margin-top: 1.4em;"}
<span class="sub">What would we want to achieve, and what would it cost to capture? Over to the discussion.</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
- Everything the other options put on screen is said aloud here: re-use is highest in HTA; a shared standard enables shared tooling for sponsors and assessors; no regulator or assessor has asked and every field has a cost.
:::
